## RRU-229

::: {.question}
RRU-229 (HEAT PUMP RATE) Velez PFT. Explain whether the proposed rate design would apply downward rate pressure for customers who do not adopt heat pump systems.

::: {.referenced-testimony}

**Velez Direct, printed p. 81, lines 10–16**

81:10  **Q. What do you propose to address the overcharging of heat pump customers?**\
81:11  **A.** I recommend that the Company create a new rate schedule, Rate HP, for residential customers\
81:12  with heat pumps. Rather than using a block design, Rate HP would lower the volumetric rates for\
81:13  distribution and transmission during the winter months (November through March), when the\
81:14  incremental heat pump load occurs. Rate 1’s summer rates, generation rates, and the fixed\
81:15  customer charge would be **unchanged**. All customers with heat pumps would be eligible to\
81:16  enroll in Rate HP, regardless of whatever heating system they had before.

**Velez Direct, printed p. 82, lines 10–12**

82:10  **A.** Rate HP would reduce distribution and transmission rates during the winter months only.\
82:11  Summer rates remain at proposed Rate 1 levels. The following table compares the Company’s\
82:12  proposed Rate 1 rates with my proposed Rate HP rates.

**Velez Direct, printed p. 83, lines 1–2**

83:1  Generation rates, the monthly customer charge, and all distribution riders remain the\
83:2  same as under Rate 1, as would summer distribution and transmission rates in the summer.[^74]

**Velez Direct, printed p. 98, lines 4–18**

98:4   **A.** Within the default rate, where revenue sufficiency must be maintained, the only way to reduce\
98:5   overcollection from heat pump customers is to raise the fixed charge on everyone, shifting\
98:6   revenue recovery away from per-kWh rates.\
98:7   And the Company could choose to create a tech-specific rate exclusively for heat pump\
98:8   customers with a high fixed-charge design. Indeed, Rate 6 takes a step in this direction, by\
98:9   raising the fixed charge from \$12.36 to \$30.95.\
98:10  But a tech-specific rate opens an additional lever for reducing overcollection that the\
98:11  default rate (or any rate that must be revenue neutral with respect to the residential class as a\
98:12  whole) does not have: keep the fixed charge the same, and simply lower volumetric charges.\
98:13  If the overcollection problem arises from the application of volumetric rates _designed for the_\
98:14  _average electric customer_ to a subclass of residential customers with structurally _above-average_\
98:15  usage, then simply lowering the volumetric rates for that population reduces overcollection from\
98:16  that population. Put another way, instead of fundamentally changing the rate design for Rate 1,\
98:17  you can simply recalibrate it, by designing the volumetric rate component for the average heat\
98:18  pump customer, rather than the average residential customer.

:::

:::

::: {.response}

## RRU-231

::: {.question}
**RRU-231 (HEAT PUMP RATE) Velez PFT, Ex. JPV-2, p. 3.** Provide evidentiary support for the claim that ResStock “systematically overstates electricity consumption for multifamily buildings.”

::: {.referenced-testimony}

**Ex. JPV-2, p. 3**

First, a **multifamily non-HVAC electricity correction.** ResStock systematically overstates electricity consumption for multifamily buildings, driven by inflated non-HVAC end uses (plug loads, lighting, appliances). The overstatement grows with a utility’s share of multifamily housing. I corrected this by scaling each multifamily building’s non-HVAC electricity consumption to match the single-family per-square-foot benchmark for each end use. HVAC loads were left unchanged.

:::

:::

::: {.response}
:::

## RRU-232

::: {.question}
**RRU-232 (HEAT PUMP RATE) Velez PFT, p. 62.** Explain why the analysis uses the AESC regional average value for bundled marginal distribution and transmission costs ($69/kW-year) rather than, for example, the Company’s MCOS study.

::: {.referenced-testimony}

**Velez Direct, printed p. 15, footnote 8**

15 n.8  of a small set of neighboring customers; and (3) upstream distribution costs (\$20.17/kW-year, system-wide), covering bulk-to-local transmission substations, local transmission lines, local-transmission-to-distribution substations, and trunkline primary feeders whose expansion is driven by growth in peak load. To calculate marginal T&D costs, I use only the third category — upstream distribution costs — because the scenario at issue is an existing customer who installs a heat pump, not a new customer connecting to the grid. Customer-related and local facilities costs are incurred when a customer first takes service; they do not change when an existing customer increases their usage. We assume fossil-fuel-heated customers already pay for customer-related and local facilities costs through their monthly bills. The only _marginal_ distribution cost that an existing customer’s incremental load can trigger, then, is the upstream cost — the cost of expanding substation and feeder capacity when peak demand grows.

**Velez Direct, printed p. 16, lines 1–3**

16:3    3. Figure 6 shows the result.

**Velez Direct, printed p. 62, lines 5–14**
